messages.subject: QUERY: Multi-species design in Distance
messages.body_plain:
--Original Message Text---
From: BSPB
Date: Mon, 2 Aug 1999 10:46:44 +0300

Hello,
My name is Boris Barov and I am new in DISTANCE. I conduct a point count
survey in
oak-pseudomaquise scrub investigating bird communities. I stratified my
observations by habitat type on the basis of structural differences in
vegetation
cover (the study area is exteremely patchy). However, I would like to know
whether
it is possible to post-stratify by species (the species composition of my
communies is of 21 species). Or maybe I should compose separate DISTANCE
project
for each species? Which is the approach recommended by DISTANCE? I am aware
that
poststratification capabilities of DISTANCE 3.5 are limited.
Hope to hear from you soon.

Yours,
Boris Barov, BSPB\BirdLife Bulgaria
--------------------------

Boris,

Your question is quite a common one, so I have sent my reply to the distance-
sampling email list as well as to you (see the "Email list" link on
http://www.ruwpa.st-and.ac.uk/distance/ if you don't know about the list).

In version 3.5 of Distance you can only stratify by one level at once.  So
you can either stratify by habitat type or by species.  However, in your case
this is not a major problem since you presumably do not wish to estimate a
combined density of "birds" over all species - instead you probably want to
estimate the density of each species separately.  In this case, set up your
project with habitat type as the stratum layer, and species name as an extra
field in the observation layer.  Then create one Data Filter for each species
you wish to analyze.  In each Data Filter, use the Data Selection tab to
include only data for that species -- for example for Robins your data filter
would include only data where layer name is "Observation", field name is
"Species", operator is "=" and value is "Robin".  To analyze data for the
Robin, you would then pair up this Data Filter with the Model Definition of
your choice.  (In the Model Definition, under Stratum Definition on the
Estimate tab you would choose the "Use stratum layer" option to stratify by
habitat.)

The alternative you suggest, using a separate project file for each species,
will also work fine.  The down side of this, however, is that you cannot
share Model Definitions among projects, so you would have to set these up
separately in each project.

Good luck with your analysis.  All the best,

 - Len Thomas

--
Len Thomas, Co-ordinator
Distance Development Project
Research Unit for Wildlife Population Assessment
Mathematical Institute, University of St Andrews
Scotland KY16 9SS

             email: dist...@mcs.st-and.ac.uk
   RUWPA home page: http://www.rupwa.st-and.ac.uk
Distance home page: http://www.rupwa.st-and.ac.uk/distance/

messages.subject: pigeonsanswers
messages.body_plain:
This is a multi-part message in MIME format. ------=_NextPart_000_0010_01BEE991.65C08C80 Content-Type: text/plain; charset="iso-8859-1" Content-Transfer-Encoding: quoted-printable Francisco Cabrera Rodr=EDguez KAV...@santandersupernet.com Hello everybody, Lask week I posted a e-mail. Now I post the answers I have received. Thanks a lot to the people that has answered!=20 I am assessing a wild pigeon population (Columba livia), I am using = enough=20 transects to see pigeons, but the first times I begun to analyze the=20 populations I only saw few flocks, (between 20 to 30); they had betweeen = 140=20 to 600 pigeons. I was wondering if I could use the bootstrap procedure = to=20 analyse the pigeons density as single instead of cluster of those first=20 pigeons. Does anyone know the answer? Thanks a lot! Hi, It is probably not a good idea to perform an analysis in which each=20 individual pigeon is considered to be an object. First, the estimation=20 routines in Distance (analytical or bootstrapping) assume that the=20 probability of detecting each object is independent of all other = objects. But=20 almost certainly you are more likely to detect an individual that is in = a=20 group of 600 hundred than you are to detect a lone individual. Treating = each=20 pigeon in a group is an independent object has the effect of making you=20 overestimate the mean detection distance for pigeons because big groups = are=20 probably detectable from farther than small groups or solitaries. This = causes=20 you to underestimate density because you are actually missing a lot more = solitaries and small groups than the detection probability estimate is=20 telling you. You also get inappropriate confidence interval estimates on = detection probability because your sample is not a random sample of = possible=20 detection distances for independently detected pigeons (as the = procedures=20 assume): you are biased towards long distances because big groups can be = detected from further. The group size effect can be handled by treating=20 groups as objects and making group detection probability a function of = group=20 size. But this does not get around the problem that you don't have a=20 sufficient sample size of groups to get a robust estimate of detection=20 probability. There is not much you can do about this besides collect = more=20 data. Sorry, Peter Walsh Hi Francisco, >From what I understand of your message, you have too few observations = from=20 your early surveys to reliably estimate a detection function and want to = increase the apparent sample size by analyzing the individuals within a=20 cluster as if they were independent observations. Sorry, but this will = not=20 help with your problem. The detection fitting procedure relies on the=20 observations being independent, and you cannot magically "create" new=20 independent observations. You will have a much larger apparent sample = size,=20 but the observations will be heavily dependent on one another. Sometimes, one is forced to analyze clustered data as individuals - for=20 example when it is hard to determine which cluster individuals are in, = or it=20 is hard to count cluster size, or it is hard to determine the centre of = the=20 cluster. When you are forced to do this, you have to be very careful = when=20 selecting a model for the detection function as the model selection=20 statistics (AIC, etc) and goodness-of-fit are all compromized. All of = these=20 assume that each observation is independent but when many observations = come=20 from the same cluster this is not the case. Bootstrapping will also not create independent observations - = boostrapping is=20 something we use to get a different (and often more reliable) variance=20 estimate and confidence limits. It cannot be used to "produce" more=20 independent observations. When you have only 20-30 observations (ie clusters) your options are: 1. Pool these observations with those from later surveys (under = comparable=20 conditions) to estimate the detection function. 2. If you have no other data to pool with, you could try fitting some = low- parameter detection functions (half-normal with up to 1 adjustment; = hazard=20 rate) and, if you have nice data with a wide shoulder and a gentle = fall-off=20 after the shoulder, you may get a decent detection function from only = these=20 few data. However, results may well not be reliable. Hope this helps, - Len Thomas P.S. It would be helpful if you could collate all the replies you get = and=20 post them as one message or summarize them to the distance-sampling list = so=20 that others can read them ------=_NextPart_000_0010_01BEE991.65C08C80 Content-Type: text/html; charset="iso-8859-1" Content-Transfer-Encoding: quoted-printable
Francisco Cabrera = Rodr=EDguez
KAV...@santandersupernet.com=
 
 
Hello everybody,
Lask week I posted a e-mail. Now I = post the=20 answers I have received.
Thanks a lot to the people that=20 has answered! 

I am assessing a wild pigeon population (Columba = livia), I=20 am using enough
transects to see pigeons, but the first times I = begun to=20 analyze the
populations I only saw few flocks, (between 20 to 30); = they had=20 betweeen 140
to 600 pigeons. I was wondering if I could use the = bootstrap=20 procedure to
analyse the pigeons density as single instead of = cluster of=20 those first
pigeons. Does anyone know the answer?
Thanks a=20 lot!


Hi,
It is probably not a good idea to perform an = analysis=20 in which each
individual pigeon is considered to be an object. = First, the=20 estimation
routines in Distance (analytical or bootstrapping) assume = that=20 the
probability of detecting each object is independent of all other = objects. But
almost certainly you are more likely to detect an = individual=20 that is in a
group of 600 hundred than you are to detect a lone = individual.=20 Treating each
pigeon in a group is an independent object has the = effect of=20 making you
overestimate the mean detection distance for pigeons = because big=20 groups are
probably detectable from farther than small groups or = solitaries.=20 This causes
you to underestimate density because you are actually = missing a=20 lot more
solitaries and small groups than the detection probability = estimate=20 is
telling you. You also get inappropriate confidence interval = estimates on=20
detection probability because your sample is not a random sample of = possible=20
detection distances for independently detected pigeons (as the = procedures=20
assume): you are biased towards long distances because big groups = can be=20
detected from further. The group size effect can be handled by = treating=20
groups as objects and making group detection probability a function = of group=20
size. But this does not get around the problem that you don't have a =
sufficient sample size of groups to get a robust estimate of = detection=20
probability. There is not much you can do about this besides collect = more=20
data.
Sorry,
Peter Walsh
Hi Francisco,

From what I understand of your = message,=20 you have too few observations from
your early surveys to reliably = estimate a=20 detection function and want to
increase the apparent sample size by=20 analyzing the individuals within a
cluster as if they were = independent=20 observations.  Sorry, but this will not
help with your = problem. =20 The detection fitting procedure relies on the
observations being=20 independent, and you cannot magically "create" new
independent=20 observations.  You will have a much larger apparent sample size, =
but=20 the observations will be heavily dependent on one = another.

Sometimes, one=20 is forced to analyze clustered data as individuals - for
example = when it is=20 hard to determine which cluster individuals are in, or it
is hard to = count=20 cluster size, or it is hard to determine the centre of the =
cluster. =20 When you are forced to do this, you have to be very careful when =
selecting a=20 model for the detection function as the model selection
statistics = (AIC,=20 etc) and goodness-of-fit are all compromized.  All of these =
assume that=20 each observation is independent but when many observations come
from = the=20 same cluster this is not the case.

Bootstrapping will also not = create=20 independent observations - boostrapping is
something we use to get a = different (and often more reliable) variance
estimate and confidence = limits.  It cannot be used to "produce" more
independent=20 observations.

When you have only 20-30 observations (ie clusters) = your=20 options are:

1. Pool these observations with those from later = surveys=20 (under comparable
conditions) to estimate the detection = function.

2.=20 If you have no other data to pool with, you could try fitting some=20 low-
parameter detection functions (half-normal with up to 1 = adjustment;=20 hazard
rate) and, if you have nice data with a wide shoulder and a = gentle=20 fall-off
after the shoulder, you may get a decent detection function = from=20 only these
few data.  However, results may well not be=20 reliable.

Hope this helps,

 - Len Thomas

P.S. = It would=20 be helpful if you could collate all the replies you get and
post = them as one=20 message or summarize them to the distance-sampling list so
that = others can=20 read them

messages.subject: sampling fraction
messages.body_plain:
Dear Distance users,

A colleague is is spotlighting nocturnal mammals in SW England and
is using Distance to estimate densities. Spotlighting from the roof
of a Land Rover is fine in most of England in that one has a 360
degree view, but in Cornwall the hedges are higher than a Land Rover
roof so he has to stop at field gates and spotlight over the gate.
Because of the variations in topography the angle of view varies
with each field. Distance offers the chance to specify the sampling
fraction, but only, as far as I can see, for a complete project. Is
there a way of specifying the sampling fraction for each sample
point? And would it be sensible to do so, even if one could?

Thanks in advance for any responses.

Mike Hounsome

Dr Mike Hounsome, Keeper of Zoology,
Manchester University Museum,
Oxford Road, Manchester, M13 9PL, UK

telephone:- 44-(0)161-275-2673

messages.subject: Re: Distance v. transect
messages.body_plain:
I had another enquiry about this (see below), so I'm posting my reply to the
list.

Question:

[...]

> >  My question is, has anyone
> >evaluated the difference between using program Distance or Transect?  Does
> >anyone have an opinion as to which would work best for the surveys I will be
> >conducting.
> >
[...]

Answer:

TRANSECT was the original software for analyzing line transect data (see
Burnham, KP, Anderson, DR, Laake JL. 1980. Estimation of density from line
transect sampling of biological populations.  Wildlife Monograph No 72).
Distance evolved from TRANSECT and supercedes it.  Distance is quite different
from its predecessor as a result of changes in analysis methods and also has
substantially expanded capibilities.  I would always recommend using Distance
over TRANSECT.  For more about the history of TRANSECT and Distance, see the
Distance web page http://www.ruwpa.st-and.ac.uk/distance/ (look under "What is
Distance").

--

messages.subject: Re: DATA FILTER error
messages.body_plain:
Jim (and anyone else with this problem),

Thanks for sending me the test project.  Your problem is that you are running
an analysis with more than 5000 samples (transects).  The analysis engine
that comes with Distance 3.5 can only cope with 5000 samples and 10000
observations.  You need to download and install the large-dataset version of
the analysis engine - you can get this from the distance web site, under
"Support, Updates and Extras".  Then everything should run fine.

You may not have realized that you were running more than 5000 samples, since
your dataset contains only 474 transects.  However, in your problematic
analysis you post-stratify by species, and there are 11 species.  When you
post-stratify by a field in the observation layer, Distance duplicates your
samples once for each post-stratum level; in your case 474x11=5214.

Also, Distance didn't give you a very informative error message (it should
have said something like "Too many samples").  Sorry about that!  Your
dataset enabled me to discover a minor bug in the analysis engine which means
that instead of exiting gracefully when there are too many samples it crashes
out.  The Distance interface therefore doesn't know what the problem was and
gives you the generic message "** Error: An error occurred within the

analysis engine. This could be due to a problem in the Distance analysis
engine, or could be because the analysis was reset just as it was finishing.

**".  We'll have this problem fixed in future releases of Distance.

I've added a note to the "Known Problems" page on the web site in case anyone
else gets a similar problem in the future.

As you said, you have a fairly complex dataset, with geographic, group size,
seasonal and species strata.  Hopefully, Distance 4 will deal with such
complex situations better than 3.5.  For one thing it will cope with multiple
levels of stratification.  For another I'm going to expand the data selection
to allow more complex queries.  However, for now, you may find yourself
having to split your dataset out into separate distance project - e.g., one
project for each species.

All the best,

 - Len Thomas

messages.subject: Choosing models by AIC or %CV
messages.body_plain:
Dear All,

I am slightly confused by some results I'm getting when
analysing some antelope data using Distance. For a
particular data set, the model with the lowest AIC value
does not necessarily have the lowest %CV. This is despite
each model being based on the same number of data points.

I realise that in general people focus on achieving lower

results with different numbers of sample points. Should I
be doing the same when choosing which model is best for
this particular data set, even if the AIC results suggests
I should use a different model?

Thanks in advance for your help.

messages.subject: Answer: Distance stratification problem
messages.body_plain:
Hi Luis,

You're not the first person to ask me about this, so I'm replying to the
distance-sampling list as well as to you.

The symptom of your problem is that whenever you try an analysis with
stratification the distance analysis engine returns the message:

** Warning: Area of each stratum has not been defined or is zero. Distance
cannot produce an abundance estimate (but will still calculate density). **

In your case, this is occuring because you changed the name of the stratum
data layer from the default "Region" to "Survey".  Nothing wrong with doing
this - in fact its a good idea to give the data layers sensible names rather
than using the defaults.  However, its easiest to do this before you start
defining and running analyses.  This is because when you change the stratum
name, Distance isn't smart enough to update the stratum definition section of
the model definitions you have already created.  So, to fix your problem you
just need to edit all the model definitions you have created that include
stratification and, on the estimate tab, under "Use stratum layer:" click on
the new stratum name in the drop down box.

In general, I'd recommend making all changes to your dataset *before* you
start defining and running analyses.
